newsitem.title: USA: Teamsters chief Carey claims re-election win.
newsitem.headline: Teamsters chief Carey claims re-election win.

text.p: Teamsters Union President Ron Carey claimed victory on Saturday in his hard-fought bid for re-election, but challenger James Hoffa said he would not concede defeat as the results were not yet official.

Court-appointed Election Officer Barbara Zack Quindel reported Carey narrowly leading Hoffa after all eligible votes were counted. But she said she could not declare the race over until additional ballots were reviewed for eligibility.
That did not stop Carey from claiming that he had won the bruising battle with the son of the late Jimmy Hoffa for the top spot of the 1.4 million-member International Brotherhood of Teamsters.
"Let me say it as it is," Carey told a news conference. "We beat the mob. We beat corporate America. We beat the old guard officials in our union."
Hoffa, 55, acknowledged that the near-final tally of votes did not look good for his campaign, but would not give up.
"This is not a time for a concession speech," he told reporters. "But it does look like it is possible Ron Carey will be elected."

The election officer, who's 500-person staff has been counting ballots since Tuesday at a rented facility in Chevy Chase, Maryland, reported Saturday night that Carey had 52 percent of the vote from the union's 560 locals. The totals were 226,593 votes for Carey and 209,896 for Hoffa.

Carey's victory margin, however, was smaller than the 41,002 outstanding so-called challenged ballots, those that have been set aside before they were processed so that their eligibility can be reviewed by the election officer.

As a result, those ballots will have to be reviewed and counted if they are found to be eligible. Quindel said the processing and counting of challenged ballots would begin Monday and would take at least a week.

Carey, 60, who said he will undergo long-delayed knee surgery on Monday, said he expects the eligible challenged ballots to reflect the same margin between him and Hoffa as the overall vote has so far shown.
If his margin of victory should fall below 3 percentage points, there will be an automatic recount.

Carey, who won the Teamster presidency as a reform candidate in the union's first open election five years ago, has fought a rough-and-tumble battle against Hoffa, whom he has accused of being backed by the mob and Teamster employers.
Hoffa's father, who ruled the union in the 1950s and 1960s before he went to prison in 1967, is presumed to have been murdered by the Mafia in 1975.
The election, only the second in the union's 93-year history, was required to be government-supervised and open to rank-and-file members under a 1989 settlement of a federal anti-racketeering suit.

It has been costly. The government-funded election has a $21 million budget. In addition, Carey said he raised $1.6 million for his campaign warchest against Hoffa's $3.7 million. The Hoffa campaign said it raised only $1.2 million.
Although Carey made some effort to extend an olive branch to his opponents, he clearly set the terms for cooperation.
"This victory sends a message to every Teamster official who has tried to undermine reform in the past five years," he said. "It's time to get on the reform train or get out of the way."

Since taking office, Carey has replaced officers of 67 Teamster locals with temporary trustees, mostly after corruption charges were raised. Hoffa and his backers said he used the tactic to silence his enemies.

If Carey's margin holds, he still will have to contend with a nearly split membership and at least five of Hoffa's running mates who won seats on the union's 24-member executive board as vice presidents from Hoffa's Midwest powerbase.
"There's a signal there that we hope that Mr. Carey should see," said Hoffa spokesman Richard Leebove. "Whoever should be the victor should try to unify this union."
Hoffa, a Detroit labor lawyer who has worked for the past three years for a Teamster joint council that was once headed by his father, was somewhat conciliatory.
"I'm more than happy to work with Ron Carey to start to rebuild this union, to start to unify this union...," he said. "But the question is what is he going to do?"
